summary: Earth Data Detectives is a web tool that helps students and the public investigate whether a NASA Earth science variable is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. The user picks a variable (such as air temperature, rainfall or soil wetness) and clicks a region on a world map. The tool gathers the monthly time series, removes the seasonal cycle, and fits a linear trend with a 95% confidence interval. It then tests significance with an autocorrelation-adjusted t-test and the Mann-Kendall test with the Theil-Sen slope. The result is a plain-language verdict, such as “decreasing by X per decade, significant”. Users can compare two regions to see trends move in opposite directions, watch a guided demo of five real-world stories, and upload their own data. This addresses the challenge by combining variable discovery, regional analysis, visualization and significance testing in one beginner-friendly tool that is honest about uncertainty and non-significant results.
details:
Project Details

What it does. The user follows four steps: choose a variable (each has a plain-language definition), choose a region on the map, view the evidence, and read the verdict. The evidence has three charts: the raw series, the average seasonal cycle, and the anomalies with the fitted trend line. Region A and region B can be shown together to reveal opposite trends. Five mission briefings and a guided demo present real-world stories: Arctic warming, a drying Aral basin, Amazon greenness, NO₂ over two megacities, and rainfall in East versus Southern Africa. Users can also upload a monthly CSV, export results, and copy a summary.

How it works. A FastAPI backend retrieves monthly NASA POWER time series for a region and caches them. A separate analysis endpoint removes the seasonal cycle, then computes an ordinary least squares trend with a 95% confidence interval, an autocorrelation-adjusted t-test, a Mann-Kendall test on annual means, and the Theil-Sen slope. A browser interface draws the charts and gives the verdict. If the backend is unavailable, the interface runs on simulated demonstration data and labels it clearly as simulated.

Benefits and impact. The tool teaches the “data detective” mindset: finding a trend, checking whether it could be chance, and being honest when evidence is weak. It supports high school and college students and members of the public with some scientific background.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, httpx, HTML, CSS and JavaScript with hand-written SVG charts.

Creativity and design. The space-themed “mission control” design, the case-file framing, side-by-side opposite trends, and a guided demo that explains results in plain language.

Limitations and next steps. The tool analyses linear trends only. The built-in briefing cases use simulated data shaped like the real stories. Next steps are real MODIS vegetation and OMI NO₂ data, trend maps with significance hatching, and non-linear trend methods.
